nodes.name: summary of the contribution
nodes.statement: We have presented a novel way to extract invariant features of $\ds$-dimensional curves, based on the iterated-integrals signature. We have identified all those features that can be written as a finite linear combination of terms in the signature.

nodes.name: building blocks of the affine integral invariants of Feng-Kogan-Krim
nodes.statement: In that work, for a curve $X: [0,T] \to \R^\ds$, $\ds=2,3$, the building blocks for invariants are expressions of the form \begin{align} \int_0^T (X^1_r)^{\alpha_1} .. (X^\ds_r)^{\alpha_\ds} dX^i_r, \qquad i=1,..,\ds. \end{align}

nodes.name: the affine integral invariants $I_1, I_2, I_3$
nodes.statement: Using an algorithmic procedure, some invariants to certain subgroups of $G \subset GL(\R^\ds)$ are derived. In particular for $\ds=2$ and $G=GL(\R^\ds)$ the following invariants are given \begin{align*} I_1 &= \frac{1}{2} \int_0^T X^1_{0,r} dX^2_r - \frac{1}{2} X^1_{0,t} X^2_{0,t} \\ I_2 &= \int_0^T X^1_{0,r} X^2_{0,r} dX^2_r\ X^1_{0,t} - \frac{1}{2} \int_0^t (X^1_r)^2 dX^2_r\ X^2_{0,t} \\ I_3 &= \int_0^T X^1_{0,r} (X^2_{0,r})^2 dX^2_r\ X^2_{0,T} - \int_0^T (X^1_{0,r})^2 X^2_{0,r} dX^2_r\ X^1_{0,T} X^2_{0,T} + \frac{1}{3} \int_0^T (X^1_{0,r})^3 dX^2_r\ X^2_{0,r} X^2_{0,r} \\ &\qquad - \frac{1}{12} (X^1_{0,t})^3 (X^2_{0,t})^3. \end{align*}

nodes.name: signature representation $\phi_1, \phi_2, \phi_3$ of $I_1, I_2, I_3$
nodes.statement: By the shuffle identity (Lemma~\ref{lem:shuffleIdentity}), we can write these as $I_i = \langle S(X)_{0,T}, \phi_i \rangle$, with \begin{align*} \phi_1 &:= \frac{1}{2} \word{12} - \frac{1}{2} \word{12} \\ \phi_2 &:= \frac13 \word{1221} +\frac13 \word{1212} -\frac23 \word{1122} +\frac13 \word{2121} +\frac13 \word{2112} -\frac23 \word{2211} \\ \phi_3 &:= - \word{121212} - \word{211122} + \word{212121} + \word{221112} - \word{121221} + \word{122211} - \word{112212} \\&\qquad + \word{122112} - \word{211212} - \word{211221} - \word{121122} + \word{122121} -3 \word{222111} +3 \word{111222} \\&\qquad+ \word{221121} + \word{212211} - \word{112122} + \word{212112} - \word{112221} + \word{221211}. \end{align*} One can easily check that these lie in the linear span of the invariants given in Proposition~\ref{prop:soInvariants} (or Theorem~\ref{thm:soInvariants}), as expected.
nodes.statement_short: The shuffle identity rewrites $I_1,I_2,I_3$ as linear signature functionals $\langle S(X)_{0,T}, \phi_i\rangle$, which lie in the span of the invariants constructed here.

nodes.name: the lemniscate of Gerono: a counterexample to completeness of integral signatures
nodes.statement: Consider the two closed curves $X^+$ and $X^-$ in $\R^2$, given for $t$ in $[0,2\pi]$ as \begin{align*} X^{\pm,1}_t &=\pm\cos t\\ X^{\pm,2}_t &=\sin 2t. \end{align*} Then all the expressions \eqref{eq:expression} coincide on $X^+$ and $X^-$.
nodes.statement_short: Two oppositely traversed lemniscates of Gerono share all values of the Feng-Kogan-Krim expressions, though their iterated-integral signatures differ.
assumptions: Consider the two closed curves $X^+$ and $X^-$ in $\R^2$, given for $t$ in $[0,2\pi]$ as
conclusions: Then all the expressions \eqref{eq:expression} coincide on $X^+$ and $X^-$.

nodes.name: Proof of the lemniscate counterexample
nodes.statement: Consider the function $f^m_n(t):=\cos^m t\;\sin^n t$, where $m$ and $n$ are nonnegative integers. If $n$ is odd, then $f^m_n(t)=-f^m_n(2\pi- t)$ so $\int_0^{2\pi}f^m_n(t)\,dt$ is zero. If $m$ is odd, then \begin{align*} \int_0^{2\pi}f^m_n(t)\,dt=-\int_{\frac\pi2}^{-\frac{3\pi}2}f^m_n(\frac\pi2-t)\,dt=\int^{\frac\pi2}_{-\frac{3\pi}2}f^n_m(t)\,dt=\int^{2\pi}_0f^n_m(t)\,dt=0. \end{align*} Thus $\int_0^{2\pi}f^m_n(t)\,dt$ can only be nonzero if $m$ and $n$ are both even. Any expression like \eqref{eq:expression} is either of the form \begin{align*} \int_0^{2\pi}x^my^n\,dx&=\int_0^{2\pi}(\pm1)^m\cos^m t\;\sin^n 2t \;(\mp\sin t)\,dt \\&=\mp2^n(\pm1)^m\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^{m+n}t\sin^{n+1}t\,dt \\&=\begin{cases}0&\text{$n$ even or $m$ even}\\-2^n\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^{m+n}t\sin^{n+1}t\,dt&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} \end{align*} or of the form \begin{align*} \int_0^{2\pi}x^my^n\,dy&=\int_0^{2\pi}(\pm1)^m\cos^m t\;\sin^n 2t \;(2\cos t)\,dt \\&=2^{n+1}(\pm1)^m\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^{m+n+1}t\;\sin^{n}t\,dt \\&=\begin{cases}0&\text{$n$ odd or $m$ odd}\\2^{n+1}\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^{m+n+1}t\;\sin^{n}t\,dt&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}. \end{align*} Therefore these two curves have the same values on terms of the form \eqref{eq:expression}. \footnote{ Note that they are not not tree-equivalent and therefore have different (iterated-integral) signatures. The lowest level on which they differ is level 4.}
nodes.statement_short: A parity argument shows the relevant trigonometric integrals vanish exactly when the sign $(\pm 1)^m$ would matter, so both traversals agree.

nodes.name: Parity of the trigonometric integrals
nodes.statement: Consider the function $f^m_n(t):=\cos^m t\;\sin^n t$, where $m$ and $n$ are nonnegative integers. If $n$ is odd, then $f^m_n(t)=-f^m_n(2\pi- t)$ so $\int_0^{2\pi}f^m_n(t)\,dt$ is zero. If $m$ is odd, then \begin{align*} \int_0^{2\pi}f^m_n(t)\,dt=-\int_{\frac\pi2}^{-\frac{3\pi}2}f^m_n(\frac\pi2-t)\,dt=\int^{\frac\pi2}_{-\frac{3\pi}2}f^n_m(t)\,dt=\int^{2\pi}_0f^n_m(t)\,dt=0. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Symmetry of $f^m_n$ kills $\int_0^{2\pi} f^m_n$ whenever $m$ or $n$ is odd.

nodes.name: Record the parity conclusion
nodes.statement: Thus $\int_0^{2\pi}f^m_n(t)\,dt$ can only be nonzero if $m$ and $n$ are both even.
nodes.statement_short: Only both-even exponents can give a nonzero integral.

nodes.name: Evaluate the two families of expressions
nodes.statement: Any expression like \eqref{eq:expression} is either of the form \begin{align*} \int_0^{2\pi}x^my^n\,dx&=\int_0^{2\pi}(\pm1)^m\cos^m t\;\sin^n 2t \;(\mp\sin t)\,dt \\&=\mp2^n(\pm1)^m\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^{m+n}t\sin^{n+1}t\,dt \\&=\begin{cases}0&\text{$n$ even or $m$ even}\\-2^n\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^{m+n}t\sin^{n+1}t\,dt&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} \end{align*} or of the form \begin{align*} \int_0^{2\pi}x^my^n\,dy&=\int_0^{2\pi}(\pm1)^m\cos^m t\;\sin^n 2t \;(2\cos t)\,dt \\&=2^{n+1}(\pm1)^m\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^{m+n+1}t\;\sin^{n}t\,dt \\&=\begin{cases}0&\text{$n$ odd or $m$ odd}\\2^{n+1}\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^{m+n+1}t\;\sin^{n}t\,dt&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}. \end{align*}

nodes.name: our method extends to any order, unlike the algorithmic construction
nodes.statement: Moreover, the algorithmic nature of the construction in \cite{bib:FKK2010} makes it difficult to proceed to invariants of higher order. In contrast, our method gives an explicit linear basis for the invariants under consideration up to \emph{any} order.

nodes.name: tree-like equivalence and the completeness question
nodes.statement: Regarding the question of whether our invariants are complete we propose the following conjecture. As shown in \cite{bib:HL2010}, if $S(X)_{0,T} = S(Y)_{0,T}$ for some curves $X,Y$, then $X$ is ``tree-like equivalent'' to $Y$. For the concrete definition of this equivalence we refer to their paper, but let us give one example. Consider in $\ds=2$, the constant path $X_t := (0,0), t \in [0,T]$ and the piecewise linear path $Y$, between the points $(0,0),(1,0)$ and $(0,0)$. One can check that \begin{align*} S(X)_{0,T} = S(Y)_{0,T} = 1. \end{align*} The signature has no chance of picking up these kind of ``excursions'' in a path; this concept is formalized in ``tree-like equivalence''. We suspect that the following holds true (with corresponding formulations for the other subgroups of $GL(\R^\ds)$).
nodes.statement_short: The signature only determines a curve up to tree-like equivalence, as the excursion example shows; this shapes the completeness conjecture.

nodes.name: completeness of the $SO$ invariants up to tree-like equivalence and rotation
nodes.statement: Let $X, Y: [0,T] \to \R^\ds$ be two curves such that \begin{align*} \Big\langle S(X)_{0,T}, \phi \Big\rangle = \Big\langle S(Y)_{0,T}, \phi \Big\rangle, \end{align*} for all $SO$ invariants given in Proposition~\ref{prop:soInvariants}. Then, there is a curve $\bar X$, tree-like equivalent to $X$, and a rotation $A \in SO(\R^d)$, such that \begin{align*} A \bar X = Y. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: If two curves agree on all $SO$ invariants, then one is a rotation of a curve tree-like equivalent to the other.

nodes.name: find a minimal generating set of the invariants inside the shuffle algebra
nodes.statement: Lastly, in Proposition~\ref{prop:glInvariants}, Proposition~\ref{prop:soInvariants} and Proposition~\ref{prop:permInvariants} we have established a linear basis for invariants for every homogeneity. As already mentioned in Remark~\ref{rem:algebraicIndependence}, owing to the shuffle identity, there are algebraic relations between elements of different homogeneity. An interesting open problem is then to find a minimal set of generators for the set of invariants, considered as a subalgebra of the shuffle algebra. (This applies to all subgroups of $GL(\R^\ds)$ and their corresponding invariants).
nodes.statement_short: The linear bases are not algebraically minimal; finding a minimal generating set of the invariants as a subalgebra of the shuffle algebra is open.
